title: The Harder Questions at the Table
subtitle: Six sessions on the questions the first hard-questions study did not answer
summary: The first hard-questions study sat with suffering, the violence in the Old Testament, the hypocrites, science, and hell. These are the other six that empty a pew and end a friendship when no one will take them seriously. Is Jesus really the only way. What about the person who never heard. What about the Bible and sexuality, where the church has so often been right in what it held and wrong in how it held it. Can we even trust the Bible we have. What about the sincerity of other religions. And is doubt itself the opposite of faith. This study is built for a table where the question is not an attack and no one has to pretend to be sure. The goal is never to win the argument. It is to keep the person at the table.
setting: A table where hard things can be said out loud. No question treated as an attack, no one required to perform certainty they do not have.
forWho: The Christian whose questions have nowhere safe to go, the skeptic willing to think out loud with honest company, and the friend who wants to be able to sit with either of them without panicking.
rhythm: Six sessions, one every week or two. Slow enough that a question can stay open between meetings without anyone rushing to close it.
leaderNote: Your job is not to win. It is to keep the person at the table. Grant the honest force of each objection before you answer it, in the form its best defenders would put it, because a person can tell when they are being handled instead of heard. Say I do not know when you do not, and say I do not have to have every answer to trust the One who does. On the sexuality session especially, lead with the church's own failures of tone before you say a word about anyone else, and speak about people who are in the room or could be, not about a category. Diagnose, never denounce.

sessions.title: Is Jesus Really the Only Way
sessions.bigIdea: The claim that Jesus is the only way is the hardest thing Christianity says to a pluralist age, and softening it into one way among many is not humility, it is a change of religion. The scandal is not that the way is narrow. It is that the way is a person who was crucified for the ones who rejected him.
sessions.open: When you first heard that Jesus is the only way to God, did it sound arrogant, or true, or both. Say honestly which, and why.
sessions.read: Read John 14:6. Jesus said to him, I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. Then read Acts 4:12. And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.
observe: Jesus does not say he shows the way or teaches the truth. What does he say he is. What is the difference.
Peter says salvation is in no one else. Notice he is standing before the same council that killed Jesus. What does that setting add to the claim.
talk: The objection at its strongest: it is offensive to say millions of sincere people of other faiths are simply wrong. Grant the force of that before you answer. Where does the offense land hardest for the person at your table.

Every faith makes exclusive claims, even the claim that all religions are the same is a claim that the ones who disagree are wrong. Is there any honest position that offends no one. Talk about why the offense cannot really be avoided, only chosen.

The Christian claim is not that Christians are better or smarter. It is that no one earns the way, that the way came down and was killed for the people who were far off. How does grace change what exclusivity even means here.
sessions.practice: This week, find one person of another faith or no faith and ask, with real curiosity and no agenda, what they actually believe and why. Listen long enough that you could state it back in a way they would sign. You cannot love a person you will not first understand.
sessions.send: The way is narrow because it is a person, not a philosophy. And the person on that narrow way came looking for the ones who were not on it.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one other believer who is afraid of this claim what you found: that the exclusivity of Jesus is not the arrogance of a club but the scandal of a grace no one earns. Then invite them to sit at this table for the next question.

sessions.title: What About Those Who Never Heard
sessions.bigIdea: The person who never heard the name of Jesus is a real and painful question, and the honest answer holds a tension rather than tidying it away. God will judge every person justly, no one will be condemned for a message they never had a chance to receive, and the Judge of all the earth will do what is right, even where we cannot see how.
sessions.open: Is there a specific person behind this question for you, a grandparent, a friend, someone in another country who died without ever hearing. Name them if you can. This is rarely only theoretical.
sessions.read: Read Genesis 18:25, where Abraham argues with God over Sodom. Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just. Then read Romans 2:14-16. For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness.
observe: Abraham does not get a full explanation from God. He gets a settled confidence about God's character. What does he trust, and what does he not get to know.
In Romans, what does Paul say is written on the heart of the person who never had the law. What does that suggest about how God deals with them.
talk: The objection at full strength: a God who condemns people for never hearing a message they had no way to hear would be a monster. Grant that. The Bible seems to grant it too, since it never says such a thing. What does that clear away.

There is a difference between saying we do not know exactly how God judges the person who never heard, and saying therefore evangelism does not matter. Hold both. Why does the mission still burn if we trust the Judge.
Notice we are more troubled by the ones who never heard than we are moved to go to the ones who have not yet. What does that reveal in us. Bring yourself into the question.
sessions.practice: Pick one person in your own life who has heard the name and never the meaning, and take one small step toward them this week, a meal, a question, an honest word. The mystery of the unreached far away should make us tender to the unreached across the street.
sessions.send: We are not given the whole map of God's justice. We are given his character, tested at a cross, and it is enough to trust him with the ones we cannot account for.
sessions.passItOn: When someone brings you this question in grief over a specific person, do not hand them a formula. Hand them the Judge of all the earth who does what is right, and sit with them. Then show one other person how to sit with it too, instead of arguing it.

sessions.title: The Bible and Sexuality
sessions.bigIdea: On sexuality the church has often been right in what it held and badly wrong in how it held it, leading with condemnation and losing the person before grace was ever spoken. Scripture holds a consistent and costly vision of marriage and the body, and it holds every one of us under the same grace, with no special category of sinner and no one beyond the reach of the washing.
sessions.open: Think of a real person, not a debate, someone you love who is somewhere the church has often handled badly. Before we say anything about what is true, say honestly how the church has made them feel. Start there.
sessions.read: Read Mark 10:6-9. But from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. Then read 1 Corinthians 6:9-11, and do not stop before the last verse. Paul lists many kinds of people who will not inherit the kingdom, and then he says, and such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
observe: In Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 6, count how many kinds of sin he names before he gets to any one you might be tempted to single out. Where does greed land on the list. Where does slander.
Look at verse 11, and such were some of you. What does the past tense do, and what does the word washed say about who this grace is for.
talk: The objection at its strongest: the church has used these verses as a weapon, singled out one sin above all others, and driven away people Jesus would have eaten with. Grant every true part of that first. Where has our tone been the sin.

Paul refuses to let anyone stand outside the list or above it. The gossip and the greedy are named right beside everyone else, and then all of us are washed together. How does that dismantle both the person who condemns and the person who feels condemned.

Truth and grace are not a slider where more of one means less of the other. Jesus was full of both at once. What would it look like to hold to what Scripture actually says and to love a specific person so well they never doubt they are wanted at your table.
sessions.practice: This week, if there is a person in your life the church has wounded here, reach out with no argument attached, only welcome. If the person at your table is the one who has felt condemned, let them hear the whole of verse 11 said over them, washed, sanctified, justified, the same grace that covers the one who is speaking.
sessions.send: The gospel never lowered the cost of following Jesus, and it never raised the price of admission to his table. Both are true, and a wounded world is waiting to meet someone who can hold them together.
sessions.passItOn: Most Christians have only ever seen this handled as a fight. Show one other believer how to handle it as a table, truth held without flinching and grace held without limit, and let them watch you love a real person well.

sessions.title: Can We Trust the Bible We Have
sessions.bigIdea: The claim that the Bible has been changed and recopied until no one knows what it first said is repeated everywhere and answered almost nowhere. The manuscript evidence is not weaker than for any other ancient book. It is stronger by a wide margin, and the honest questions about copying and translation have honest answers.
sessions.open: Where did you first hear that the Bible has been changed over the centuries. Did anyone ever show you the evidence either way, or was it just something everyone seemed to know.
sessions.read: Read 2 Timothy 3:16. All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness. Then read Luke 1:1-4, where Luke tells us how he worked. Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account, that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.
observe: Luke does not claim a vision dropped in his lap. What does he say he actually did, and who did he say his sources were.
What is Luke's stated goal for his reader in verse 4. What word does he use for what he wants them to have.
talk: The objection at its strongest: like a game of telephone, the text must have drifted over two thousand years. Grant why that sounds reasonable. Then consider that we have thousands of early copies to compare, so drift is not hidden, it is measurable, and where copies differ it is almost always in spelling, not in anything a doctrine stands on.

Translation is a real and honest question. A person can read four English Bibles side by side and see the differences in the open, which is the opposite of a cover up. How does having many translations actually build trust rather than undermine it.

Underneath the manuscript question is usually a deeper one, whether a person wants the book to be reliable. Be honest at the table about the difference between an intellectual objection and a wish. Which is doing the work in you.
sessions.practice: This week, read the same short passage in three different translations, side by side, and write down what actually changes and what does not. Bring what you find back to the table. Nothing builds confidence like looking with your own eyes instead of trusting a rumor.
sessions.send: The Bible is not a fragile thing we must protect from questions. It is the most examined book in human history, and it has survived the examination. Bring your hardest look. It can take it.
sessions.passItOn: Teach one other person the side by side method, three translations of one passage. A believer who has looked with their own eyes stops being afraid of the rumor, and starts being able to answer it for someone else.

sessions.title: What About the Other Religions
sessions.bigIdea: Taking other religions seriously does not mean pretending they all say the same thing, which is a quiet insult to every one of them. It means honoring the real devotion in them, telling the truth about where they genuinely differ, and letting the resurrection be the thing that is either false or changes everything.
sessions.open: What is a religion other than your own that you actually admire something about. Name the real thing you respect in it before we talk about any difference.
sessions.read: Read Acts 17:22-31, Paul at Athens. So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said, Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. He does not mock their altars. He quotes their own poets. And then he turns a corner. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world by a man whom he has appointed, and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.
observe: How does Paul begin with the people of Athens. What does he affirm, and whose words does he quote back to them.
Where is the hinge of the whole speech. Find the single fact Paul puts everything on at the end.
talk: The objection at its strongest: it is narrow and Western to say one faith is true and the rest are mistaken. Grant that arrogance is a real danger. Then notice that saying all religions are basically the same erases what each of them actually teaches, which is its own kind of disrespect. Which is more honoring to a devout person, agreement or honest engagement.

Paul does not argue his way from their altars to the resurrection by philosophy. He lands the whole thing on a historical claim, that a man was raised. Why does he make it stand or fall on that instead of on which religion is nicer.

The religions genuinely differ on the biggest things, who God is, what is wrong with us, what the rescue is. Talk about one real difference, not to score, but so no one at the table thinks honesty is the same as contempt.
sessions.practice: This week, learn one true thing about a faith you know little about, from a person or a good source, not a caricature. Honesty about others is part of loving them, and you cannot commend Jesus to a person whose beliefs you were never willing to understand.
sessions.send: Christianity does not rest on being the most reasonable religion in the room. It rests on an empty tomb. If that did not happen, walk away. If it did, everything else is a footnote.
sessions.passItOn: Show one other believer how to honor another faith and still tell the truth, beginning where Paul began, with real respect, and landing where Paul landed, on the resurrection. Then send them to have one honest conversation of their own.

sessions.title: Is Doubt the Opposite of Faith
sessions.bigIdea: Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Unbelief that refuses to look is. Thomas doubted out loud, in the room, to the others, and Jesus did not throw him out. He showed him his hands. The table is the place a question can stay safe long enough for the answer to come.
sessions.open: What is a doubt you have carried and never said out loud in church because you were afraid of the look on someone's face. You do not have to answer it tonight. Just say it exists.
sessions.read: Read John 20:24-29. Thomas says, unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark, I will never believe. Eight days later Jesus comes and says to Thomas, put your finger here, and see my hands. Do not disbelieve, but believe. Then read Mark 9:24, the father of the boy, who cries out and says, I believe, help my unbelief.
observe: Where was Thomas when he doubted, and who was he with. What does it matter that he stayed in the room instead of leaving.

The father in Mark 9 says two things in one breath, I believe and help my unbelief. Can both be true at once in the same person. What does that do to the idea that you must be certain to come to Jesus.
talk: Grant the honest fear first: many churches have treated doubt as disloyalty, so people take their questions and leave to keep them. Where have we made the table unsafe for the honest question. Bring ourselves in.
Jesus meets Thomas with evidence, his actual wounds, not with a rebuke for wanting it. What does that say about whether God is threatened by our questions.

There is a difference between the doubt that stays in the room to wrestle and the unbelief that has decided in advance not to look. Talk about which one you are carrying right now, honestly, and which one the person across from you is.
sessions.practice: This week, be the safe room for one person's doubt. Ask someone what they are actually wrestling with, and receive it without flinching, correcting, or fixing. A doubt spoken at a table that does not panic is halfway to being healed.
sessions.send: Bring your doubt into the room. Say it out loud to people who will not leave. That is not the failure of faith. It is often how faith survives.
sessions.passItOn: The greatest gift you can give a doubting friend is a table that will not throw them out. Become that table for one person, and teach them, by how you receive their questions, how to receive someone else's.
